sections.normalized_html: If [MATH: \csc x = 8,] then what is [MATH: \csc(x-8\pi)?]
sections.readable_text: If [MATH: \csc x = 8,] then what is [MATH: \csc(x-8\pi)?]

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
The period of [MATH: y = \csc x] is [MATH: 2\pi.] Therefore, for integer [MATH: n] we have

[MATH: \csc{x} = \csc{(x+2n\pi)} .]

Substituting [MATH: n=-4] into the right-hand-side of the above gives

[MATH: \csc x|= \csc (x + 2 ⋅ (− 4) ⋅ π); = \csc (x − 8π).]

Therefore, if [MATH: \csc{x} = 8,] then [MATH: \csc{(x-8\pi)} = 8.]

Content:
Recall that a function [MATH: f(x)] is odd if it satisfies the property

Content:
[MATH: f(-x) = -f(x).]

Content:
As it turns out, cosecant is an odd function! So, for any value of [MATH: x,] we have
[MATH: \csc(-x) = -\csc(x).]

Content:
Odd functions always have rotational symmetry of order [MATH: 2] about the origin. This is indeed true of the cosecant function, as we can see from the diagram below.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/6511ba7717b414bd1b6e27a0b2eab208]

Content:
We can use the oddness property of cosecant in conjunction with its periodicity property to simplify trigonometric expressions. Let's see an example.

items.title: Utilizing the Oddness Property of the Cosecant Function

sections.normalized_html: If [MATH: \csc{x} = \dfrac{7}{2},] then find the value of [MATH: \csc(-x - 20\pi).]
sections.readable_text: If [MATH: \csc{x} = \dfrac{7}{2},] then find the value of [MATH: \csc(-x - 20\pi).]

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
First, let's recall the graph of [MATH: y = \csc{x}.]

From the graph, we note the following:

  • The period of [MATH: \csc{x}] is [MATH: 2\pi.]

  • Our graph has rotational symmetry of order [MATH: 2] about the origin. This means that [MATH: \csc{x}] is an odd function, and we have [MATH: \csc(-x) = -\csc{x}.]

Let's now evaluate our expression:

  • Firstly, using the periodicity of [MATH: \csc{x},] we have [MATH: \csc (− x − 20π)|= \csc (− x − 2π ⋅ 10); = \csc (− x).]

  • Secondly, using the oddness of [MATH: \csc{x},] we have [MATH: \csc (− x)|= − \csc x; = − (7)/(2).]

Therefore, [MATH: \csc(-x - 20\pi) = -\dfrac{7}{2}.]

Item 6 — Example: Utilizing the Periodicity Property of the Cosecant Function

Example Prompt:

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
The period of [MATH: y = \csc x] is [MATH: 2\pi.] Therefore, for integer [MATH: n] we have

[MATH: \csc{x} = \csc{(x+2n\pi)} .]

Substituting [MATH: n=-4] into the right-hand-side of the above gives

[MATH: \csc x|= \csc (x + 2 ⋅ (− 4) ⋅ π); = \csc (x − 8π).]

Therefore, if [MATH: \csc{x} = 8,] then [MATH: \csc{(x-8\pi)} = 8.]

Item 10 — Example: Utilizing the Oddness Property of the Cosecant Function

Example Prompt:
If [MATH: \csc{x} = \dfrac{7}{2},] then find the value of [MATH: \csc(-x - 20\pi).]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
First, let's recall the graph of [MATH: y = \csc{x}.]

[IMG: /graphics/8c39f3895fd26e9d53a573809cdb9ee3]

From the graph, we note the following:

- The period of [MATH: \csc{x}] is [MATH: 2\pi.]
- Our graph has rotational symmetry of order [MATH: 2] about the origin. This means that [MATH: \csc{x}] is an odd function, and we have
[MATH: \csc(-x) = -\csc{x}.]

Let's now evaluate our expression:

- Firstly, using the periodicity of [MATH: \csc{x},] we have
[MATH: \csc (− x − 20π)|= \csc (− x − 2π ⋅ 10); = \csc (− x).]
- Secondly, using the oddness of [MATH: \csc{x},] we have
[MATH: \csc (− x)|= − \csc x; = − (7)/(2).]

Therefore, [MATH: \csc(-x - 20\pi) = -\dfrac{7}{2}.]
